questions.stem: Same PACU patient with TOF ratio 0.5: why does residual block cause hypoxemia and aspiration risk even when tidal volumes look adequate?
options: Hypoxic ventilatory drive is enhanced by residual block
The diaphragm is fully paralyzed at this level
questions.explanation: Pharyngeal muscles are sensitive to residual block, so airway patency and swallowing remain impaired even with adequate diaphragm function; residual block also blunts the hypoxic ventilatory response. The diaphragm is relatively resistant. Bronchial smooth muscle isn't affected by NMBs.

questions.stem: Same PACU patient with residual block. Which intraoperative drugs could have contributed? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides and magnesium reduce ACh release and potentiate nondepolarizing block. Ondansetron, dexamethasone, acetaminophen, and glycopyrrolate don't potentiate block.

questions.stem: Patient with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg every 4 hr is having thymectomy. What is the most common morning-of-surgery plan?
options: Replace it with IV neostigmine at induction to avoid weakness
Double the pyridostigmine dose to prevent crisis
questions.explanation: Most centers continue pyridostigmine to avoid weakness, accepting that it may alter relaxant and cholinesterase-dependent drug effects. Doubling risks cholinergic crisis. Stopping risks myasthenic crisis. IV neostigmine at induction isn't standard.

questions.stem: Same myasthenia patient needs a nondepolarizing relaxant. Which plan is BEST?
options: Cisatracurium at double the usual dose
Small titrated rocuronium doses with monitoring
Pancuronium for stable relaxation with neostigmine reversal
questions.explanation: Myasthenic patients are sensitive to NDMRs, so small doses (often 10–20% of usual) guided by monitoring, with sugammadex to reverse, are safest. Standard or doubled doses risk prolonged block. Pancuronium is long-acting and hard to reverse.

questions.stem: Same myasthenia patient after surgery received extra neostigmine: now weak with fasciculations, salivation, miosis, and HR 48. Interpretation?
questions.explanation: Weakness with muscarinic signs (salivation, miosis, bradycardia) and fasciculations points to excess acetylcholine. Myasthenic crisis lacks muscarinic signs. Residual block doesn't cause salivation or miosis. Lambert-Eaton is a different disease.

questions.stem: Same myasthenia patient. Which factors predict the need for postoperative ventilation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Longer disease duration, high pyridostigmine requirement, and low vital capacity (along with chronic lung disease) predict postoperative ventilation. Young age, ocular-only disease, and sex don't raise risk.

questions.stem: Teen received sevoflurane and succinylcholine; masseter rigidity occurred but surgery continued. 30 min later EtCO2 is 58 despite doubled ventilation, HR 135. What should happen with the machine?
options: Keep sevoflurane at 0.5 MAC to avoid awareness
Change the anesthesia machine before giving dantrolene
High fresh gas flow and charcoal filters
questions.explanation: Triggers are stopped immediately, high fresh gas flow washes out vapor, and activated charcoal filters speed this; treatment shouldn't wait for a machine change. Any volatile, including desflurane, continues to trigger MH.

questions.stem: Same MH patient: ABG pH 7.12, PaCO2 70, K+ 6.8 with peaked T waves. Which treatments for the hyperkalemia are appropriate? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Calcium stabilizes the myocardium, insulin shifts potassium, and correcting respiratory acidosis helps. Calcium channel blockers with dantrolene can cause hyperkalemia and collapse. Digoxin and succinylcholine worsen the situation.

questions.stem: Same MH patient is being actively cooled. At what core temperature should active cooling stop?
questions.explanation: Active cooling stops around 38–38.5 °C to avoid overshoot hypothermia. 36–37 °C targets risk overshoot. 39.5 °C is still dangerously high.

questions.stem: Same 60 kg MH patient needs three doses of dantrolene at 2.5 mg/kg. How many 20 mg vials?
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 60 = 150 mg per dose × 3 = 450 mg. 450 ÷ 20 = 22.5, so 23 vials. 8 vials covers one dose. 45 vials doubles the total. 3 vials treats each dose as one vial.

questions.stem: Same MH patient after control: CK is rising and urine is dark. What is the main goal for renal protection?
options: Restrict fluids to avoid pulmonary edema from dantrolene
Alkalinize urine with bicarbonate before giving fluids
Fluids to keep urine output high
questions.explanation: Myoglobinuria risks kidney injury, so fluids (with diuretics if needed) target high urine output. Fluid restriction increases injury. Dialysis is reserved for established failure or refractory hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: 5-year-old with obstructive sleep apnea is having tonsillectomy. Which analgesic should be AVOIDED for discharge?
questions.explanation: Codeine is contraindicated in children under 12 after tonsillectomy because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers convert it to morphine unpredictably, causing deaths. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen are standard. Carefully dosed oxycodone avoids the genetic conversion problem, though caution still applies with OSA.

questions.stem: Same 20 kg child for tonsillectomy. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is ordered. What dose?
questions.explanation: 0.15 × 20 = 3 mg. 0.3 is a decimal slip. 30 mg is tenfold too much. 1.5 mg uses 0.075 mg/kg.

questions.stem: Same child after tonsillectomy: thrashing and inconsolable at emergence; SpO2 98%, no obstruction. Which drug is BEST if one is needed?
questions.explanation: Dex reduces emergence delirium with minimal respiratory depression. Midazolam can worsen agitation in some children. Physostigmine is for anticholinergic syndrome. Ketamine can itself cause emergence reactions.

questions.stem: Same child returns 8 hr later bleeding from the tonsil bed, HR 150, pale. Which induction plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Rapid sequence with a reduced induction dose
Inhalation induction with sevoflurane in the lateral position
questions.explanation: The child has a full stomach of blood and hypovolemia, so a rapid sequence induction with a hemodynamically gentle dose and suction ready is standard. Mask induction risks aspiration. Awake fiberoptic isn't feasible in a child. An LMA doesn't protect the airway.

questions.stem: After vaginal delivery, EBL is 1,200 mL and the uterus is boggy despite an oxytocin infusion. She has chronic hypertension (BP 150/95) and no asthma. Which TWO actions are BEST now? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: With hypertension, carboprost is the next uterotonic, and TXA within 3 hr of birth reduces death from bleeding. Methylergonovine worsens hypertension. A large oxytocin push causes hypotension. Terbutaline and nitroglycerin relax the uterus.

questions.stem: Same hemorrhage: EBL reaches 2,500 mL, HR 130, BP 78/40. Massive transfusion is activated. Which ratio is the usual starting target?
options: PRBC alone until coagulation labs return
FFP first, then PRBC once INR is normal
questions.explanation: Balanced resuscitation near 1:1:1 limits dilutional coagulopathy; obstetric protocols often add early fibrinogen. Waiting for labs or giving mostly PRBCs worsens coagulopathy. Delaying red cells in shock is unsafe.

questions.stem: Same hemorrhage patient goes to laparotomy for persistent atony under GA. How should the anesthetic be adjusted?
options: Keep volatile under about 0.5 MAC or use TIVA
Avoid opioids to protect uterine tone
Use 1.5 MAC volatile to blunt the stress response
Use desflurane at high concentration for fast washout
questions.explanation: Volatiles relax uterine smooth muscle in a dose-related way, so low concentrations or a propofol-based technique preserve tone. Higher volatile doses worsen atony. Opioids don't affect uterine tone and help stabilize hemodynamics.

questions.stem: Same patient: TXA 1 g is diluted in 100 mL to run over 10 min. What pump rate?
questions.explanation: 100 mL over 10 min = 10 mL/min × 60 = 600 mL/hr. 100 runs it over an hour. 10 is the per-minute rate mislabeled. 60 is a decimal slip.

questions.stem: Preeclampsia with BP 172/112, platelets 48,000, and fetal bradycardia requires GA cesarean. BP has been treated with labetalol. Which drug BEST blunts the laryngoscopy pressor response?
questions.explanation: The hypertensive response to laryngoscopy can cause intracranial hemorrhage in preeclampsia; remifentanil 0.5–1 mcg/kg acts fast and wears off quickly (alert neonatology for possible neonatal depression). 25 mcg fentanyl is too little. Hydralazine is too slow. Midazolam doesn't blunt the response.

questions.stem: Same preeclampsia patient is on magnesium. Which RSI relaxant plan is BEST?
options: No relaxant, using remifentanil 1 mcg/kg alone
questions.explanation: Magnesium potentiates maintenance doses, but intubating doses stay standard for reliable conditions. 0.3 mg/kg rocuronium or 0.5 mg/kg succinylcholine gives poor intubating conditions. Relaxant-free intubation is less reliable in an emergency cesarean.

questions.stem: Same preeclampsia patient needs a magnesium load of 4 g over 20 min. The bag is 20 g in 500 mL. What pump rate?
questions.explanation: 20 g/500 mL = 40 mg/mL. 4,000 mg ÷ 40 = 100 mL over 20 min. 100 × 3 = 300 mL/hr. 100 mL/hr runs it over an hour. 12 and 30 are unit or decimal errors.

questions.stem: Same preeclampsia patient after delivery: the uterus is atonic despite oxytocin. She has no asthma. Which uterotonic should be AVOIDED?
questions.explanation: Methylergonovine's vasoconstriction can cause hypertensive crisis and stroke in preeclampsia. Carboprost, misoprostol, and oxytocin infusion are acceptable.

questions.stem: Spinal for cesarean with bupivacaine 12 mg, fentanyl, and morphine 100 mcg. A prophylactic phenylephrine infusion is planned. What starting rate is typical?
questions.explanation: Prophylactic phenylephrine is usually started near 25–50 mcg/min and titrated to baseline BP and HR. 1–2 mcg/min is too low to prevent hypotension. 200–300 mcg/min risks hypertension and bradycardia. The last option uses the wrong units.

questions.stem: Same cesarean spinal: within 5 min the patient says her hands tingle and her grip is weak; speech is faint and SpO2 92%. What is the BEST step?
options: Raise her head to stop spread
Give naloxone for the intrathecal opioid
Prepare to intubate for a high spine
questions.explanation: Upper extremity weakness and difficulty speaking suggest block reaching cervical levels, and airway and breathing support (often intubation) is needed. This isn't expected. Elevating the head doesn't reliably limit spread and can worsen hypotension. Naloxone doesn't reverse local anesthetic block.

questions.stem: Same healthy cesarean patient (no OSA, no added sedatives) received intrathecal morphine 100 mcg. What respiratory monitoring does SOAP consensus suggest?
options: RR and sedation every 3 hr for 12 hr
Hourly for 12 hr, then every 2 hr for 12 hr
Continuous capnography and pulse oximetry for 72 hr
No added monitoring beyond routine postop care
questions.explanation: SOAP's 2019 consensus statement tiers monitoring by dose and risk. For low-dose intrathecal morphine (over 50 up to 150 mcg) in healthy patients, it adds respiratory rate and sedation checks every 3 hr for 12 hr to routine postoperative care. Hourly checks for 12 hr then every 2 hr for 12 hr apply to high doses (over 150 mcg) or any high-risk patient, such as OSA or added sedatives. Routine care alone applies to ultra-low doses (50 mcg or less). Continuous monitoring for 72 hr far exceeds any recommendation.
questions.citation: Bauchat JR, Weiniger CF, Sultan P, et al. Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology consensus statement: monitoring recommendations for prevention and detection of respiratory depression associated with administration of neuraxial morphine for cesarean delivery analgesia. Anesth Analg. 2019;129(2):458-474.

questions.stem: Epidural test dose: 3 mL of 1.5% lidocaine with epinephrine. Within 3 min the legs feel heavy and warm, and BP falls. HR is unchanged. Interpretation?
questions.explanation: Rapid motor block and hypotension after a small lidocaine dose indicate subarachnoid spread. Intravascular injection raises HR from the epinephrine. A correctly placed epidural doesn't produce motor block this quickly. Vasovagal reactions don't cause leg weakness.

questions.stem: Pregnant patient in cardiac arrest from local anesthetic toxicity: CPR, lipid, and left uterine displacement are underway. When should delivery of the fetus begin?
questions.explanation: Resuscitative cesarean should begin around 4 min to deliver by 5 min; emptying the uterus improves venous return and maternal survival. Waiting longer or for ROSC worsens outcomes.

questions.stem: Same pregnant patient weighs 90 kg. Using current local anesthetic toxicity guidance, what is the initial 20% lipid bolus?
questions.explanation: ASRA's 2020 LAST checklist gives patients over 70 kg a fixed bolus of 100 mL 20% lipid over 2–3 min, then 200–250 mL over 15–20 min; under 70 kg it uses 1.5 mL/kg (lean body weight) then 0.25 mL/kg/min. 135 mL applies the under-70-kg formula to total weight. 13.5 mL is a decimal slip. 225 mL uses 2.5 mL/kg. The dosing limit is about 12 mL/kg.
questions.citation: Neal JM, Neal EJ, Weinberg GL. American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine local anesthetic systemic toxicity checklist: 2020 version. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2021;46(1):81-82.

questions.stem: Labor epidural with bupivacaine 0.125% and fentanyl. Two hours later the patient is hypotensive with bilateral dense motor block to T6. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Catheter migration into the intrathecal space
Opioid overdose from accumulating epidural fentanyl
Normal spread of a labor dose
questions.explanation: Dense motor block to a high level from a dilute labor solution suggests the catheter has migrated intrathecally. A correctly placed epidural with dilute bupivacaine shouldn't do this. LAST causes CNS and cardiac signs. Fentanyl doesn't cause motor block.

questions.stem: Patient at 24 weeks' gestation is recovering from laparoscopic appendectomy. Which analgesic should be AVOIDED?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs after about 20 weeks can cause fetal renal dysfunction with oligohydramnios and, later, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. Acetaminophen, carefully dosed opioids, and regional blocks are acceptable.

questions.stem: Same patient at 24 weeks needs positioning for surgery. Why is left uterine displacement used?
questions.explanation: After about 20 weeks, the uterus can compress the vena cava and aorta in the supine position, lowering preload and uteroplacental flow. The other options aren't the purpose.

questions.stem: TBI patient under GA for craniotomy: ICP 30, CPP 55, PaCO2 40. Which measures are appropriate right now? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Head elevation improves venous drainage, osmotherapy reduces brain water, brief hyperventilation lowers CBF as a bridge, and propofol lowers CMRO2 and CBF. Volatiles above 1 MAC dilate cerebral vessels. Nitroglycerin raises cerebral blood volume.

questions.stem: Same TBI patient: MAP 60 after hemorrhage elsewhere; ICP is high. Which osmotic agent is preferred, and why?
options: Mannitol; it doesn't cross an intact blood-brain barrier
Mannitol; it raises BP through diuresis
Furosemide; it lowers ICP without volume loss
questions.explanation: In a hypotensive patient, hypertonic saline lowers ICP while supporting intravascular volume. Mannitol's diuresis can worsen hypovolemia and CPP. Mannitol's barrier exclusion is true but doesn't address hypotension. Furosemide causes volume loss.

questions.stem: Same 70 kg TBI patient needs phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV, given no faster than 50 mg/min. What is the shortest safe infusion time?
questions.explanation: 20 × 70 = 1,400 mg. 1,400 ÷ 50 = 28 min. 2.8 is a decimal slip. 14 min uses 100 mg/min. 40 min uses 35 mg/min.

questions.stem: Same TBI patient on levetiracetam needs ongoing seizure prophylaxis. Why is levetiracetam often chosen over phenytoin?
options: Faster onset as an IV push
It also lowers ICP through reduced metabolism
questions.explanation: Levetiracetam lacks phenytoin's enzyme induction, protein binding issues, and narrow therapeutic range, so routine levels aren't needed; that practical advantage drives its use, although the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition found insufficient evidence that it is more effective than phenytoin for early seizure prevention. Onset isn't the main advantage. It doesn't lower ICP or affect relaxants.
questions.citation: Carney N, Totten AM, O'Reilly C, et al. Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, fourth edition. Neurosurgery. 2017;80(1):6-15.

questions.stem: Posterior spine fusion with motor evoked potential monitoring. Which anesthetic plan BEST preserves MEP signals?
options: Isoflurane 1.2 MAC with a cisatracurium infusion
questions.explanation: MEPs are sensitive to volatile anesthetics and nitrous oxide and are abolished by neuromuscular blockade, so TIVA without ongoing relaxant is standard. Each distractor combines a volatile with nitrous oxide or a relaxant.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Spine surgery with motor evoked potentials

questions.stem: Same spine patient: MEP amplitudes fall 60% bilaterally during correction. Which anesthetic and physiologic responses are appropriate? (Select 3)
options: Check for recent anesthetic boluses or depth changes
questions.explanation: Spinal cord perfusion, anesthetic changes, hypothermia, and anemia all affect MEPs and should be corrected while the surgeon assesses the correction. Relaxants and volatiles depress signals. Lowering MAP threatens cord perfusion.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Spine surgery with motor evoked potentials

questions.stem: Same spine patient needs an analgesic adjunct that is LEAST likely to depress MEPs. Which is BEST?
questions.explanation: Ketamine tends to preserve or enhance evoked potential amplitudes. Benzodiazepine boluses, volatiles, and nitrous oxide depress MEPs.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Spine surgery with motor evoked potentials

questions.stem: Same spine fusion patient takes oxycodone 60 mg/day. Which intraoperative opioid choice may reduce postoperative opioid needs for days?
questions.explanation: Methadone's long half-life and NMDA antagonism provide prolonged analgesia and have reduced postoperative opioid use in spine surgery trials. High-dose remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia. A large morphine bolus at closure risks respiratory depression. Meperidine isn't appropriate.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Spine surgery with motor evoked potentials

questions.stem: 85 kg patient is going on bypass. Heparin 400 units/kg is drawn from 1,000 units/mL vials. What volume?
questions.explanation: 400 × 85 = 34,000 units ÷ 1,000 units/mL = 34 mL. 3.4 and 340 mL are decimal errors. 25.5 mL uses 300 units/kg. Confirm adequacy with an ACT of at least about 400–480 sec before bypass.

questions.stem: Same bypass candidate developed HIT confirmed by antibody and functional assay 3 weeks ago, and surgery can't wait. Which anticoagulant is BEST for bypass?
questions.explanation: With active or recent HIT antibodies, a direct thrombin inhibitor such as bivalirudin avoids heparin re-exposure. Heparin and LMWH can trigger thrombosis. Warfarin isn't a bypass anticoagulant.

questions.stem: Same CABG patient after bypass: MAP 50, cardiac index 3.2, SVR 600, on norepinephrine 0.2 mcg/kg/min. Which drug is BEST next?
questions.explanation: High output with very low SVR is vasoplegia; vasopressin restores tone through a non-adrenergic pathway. Dobutamine and milrinone dilate vessels further. More catecholamine adds arrhythmia risk without addressing the mechanism.

questions.stem: Same CABG patient with vasoplegia remains hypotensive on norepinephrine and vasopressin. He takes sertraline. Which rescue is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Methylene blue is a potent MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; hydroxocobalamin is an alternative that scavenges nitric oxide. Nitroprusside dilates vessels. A 1 mg phenylephrine bolus is excessive and unlikely to solve the problem.

questions.stem: Same CABG patient is bleeding after protamine. Match each TEG finding to the MOST appropriate product.
prompts: Reduced alpha angle with low fibrinogen
questions.explanation: R time reflects clotting factor activity, MA mostly platelet function, alpha angle fibrinogen, and LY30 fibrinolysis. Protamine treats residual heparin, typically shown by an R time that corrects with heparinase.

questions.stem: Patient with pheochromocytoma is being prepared for surgery. Which findings suggest adequate preoperative alpha blockade? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Controlled seated BP, mild orthostasis, and nasal congestion suggest effective alpha blockade. Resting tachycardia, ischemic changes, and ongoing paroxysms suggest inadequate preparation.

questions.stem: Same pheochromocytoma patient: during tumor manipulation, BP jumps to 240/130 with HR 104. Which drug is BEST?
questions.explanation: A titratable vasodilator (clevidipine, nitroprusside, or phentolamine) controls catecholamine surges quickly. Labetalol is mostly beta blocking IV and may not control alpha surges. Hydralazine is slow and long-acting. Esmolol alone risks unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Same pheochromocytoma patient: after the adrenal vein is ligated, BP falls to 70/40. Which steps are appropriate? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Catecholamine levels fall abruptly after ligation, unmasking vasodilation and volume deficit; vasodilators stop, volume and pressors are given, and glucose is checked. More vasodilator or beta blockade worsens hypotension.

questions.stem: Same pheochromocytoma patient: why can hypoglycemia occur after tumor removal?
options: Labetalol causes direct hypoglycemia through beta-2 blockade
The adrenal gland stops producing glucagon
questions.explanation: Catecholamines suppress insulin release; when they drop, insulin rebounds while glycogen stores may be depleted. The adrenal medulla doesn't make glucagon. The other explanations aren't the mechanism.

questions.stem: Trauma patient 1 hr after injury: SBP 70, HR 140, massive transfusion activated. What TXA regimen is standard?
options: 2 g over 1 hr starting at 6 hr
1 g bolus if fibrinogen is low
1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hr
questions.explanation: Trial data support 1 g over 10 min within 3 hr of injury, then 1 g over 8 hr. Waiting for labs or starting after 3 hr loses benefit. 100 mg/kg is a cardiac surgery-style dose, not the trauma regimen.

questions.stem: Same trauma patient after 10 units of blood: K+ 6.4 with peaked T waves, iCa 0.9. Which factors contribute? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Stored red cells leak potassium, citrate binds calcium and worsens potassium's cardiac effects, and acidosis shifts potassium out of cells. Blood products contain citrate, not excess calcium. Hypothermia doesn't raise calcium. FFP doesn't lower potassium enough to matter.

questions.stem: Same trauma patient's core temperature is 34 °C. Coagulation tests run at 37 °C are near normal, but oozing continues. Why?
options: Labs warm the sample and miss hypothermic clotting dysfunction
The PT is falsely prolonged by cold samples
Hypothermia speeds clotting, so oozing isn't from coagulopathy
questions.explanation: Clotting enzymes and platelets work poorly in the cold, but standard labs warm samples to 37 °C and can look normal. Active warming is part of hemostatic resuscitation. Hypothermia impairs, not speeds, clotting.

questions.stem: Same trauma patient: fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL. Which product raises fibrinogen MOST efficiently?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen; a typical adult pool raises it substantially. FFP contains fibrinogen at plasma levels and needs large volumes. Platelets and PCC don't meaningfully raise fibrinogen.

questions.stem: Patient with untreated Graves disease is under GA for appendectomy: AF at 160, temp 39.5 °C, EtCO2 48, no rigidity, CK normal. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia and tachyarrhythmia with only mild hypercarbia, no rigidity, and normal CK in a patient with untreated hyperthyroidism point to thyroid storm. MH typically shows a sharp EtCO2 rise, rigidity, and rising CK. NMS follows dopamine antagonists. Sepsis is possible but doesn't explain the full picture.

questions.stem: Same patient in thyroid storm under GA. Which treatments are appropriate? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Beta blockade controls adrenergic effects, PTU blocks synthesis and peripheral conversion, hydrocortisone also blocks conversion and covers relative adrenal insufficiency, and cooling treats hyperthermia. Aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins. Iodine is given at least an hour after the thionamide.

questions.stem: Same thyroid storm patient. Why is acetaminophen preferred to aspirin for fever?
options: Acetaminophen also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion
It frees T4 and T3 from binding proteins
questions.explanation: Salicylates free bound thyroid hormone and can worsen storm. Acetaminophen doesn't block conversion; it's simply safer. The other options aren't real effects.

questions.stem: ESRD patient missed dialysis; K+ 6.6 with peaked T waves. He needs a fistula declot that could wait a few hours. What is the BEST plan?
options: Proceed under MAC because no relaxant is needed
Give kayexalate and proceed immediately under MAC
questions.explanation: With ECG changes, potassium needs urgent treatment, and dialysis is definitive; a semi-elective procedure can wait. Proceeding exposes the patient to arrhythmia risk. Oral binders act too slowly.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: ESRD with hyperkalemia for fistula declot

questions.stem: Same ESRD patient with K+ 6.6. Insulin with dextrose is planned. What insulin dose is often recommended in kidney failure to reduce hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation: Insulin clearance falls in kidney failure. A retrospective cohort of 675 ED patients with renal insufficiency found 5 units lowered potassium as much as 10 units with less hypoglycemia (19.5% vs 28.6%), and a quality improvement study saw less severe hypoglycemia after switching ESRD patients to 5 units. In moderate CKD the data are mixed: one study found 10 units lowered potassium about 0.3 mmol/L more without more hypoglycemia. Glucose checks for several hours are still needed. 20 units risks severe hypoglycemia, SC glargine is too slow, and 0.5 units is ineffective.
questions.citation: LaRue HA, Peksa GD, Shah SC. A comparison of insulin doses for the treatment of hyperkalemia in patients with renal insufficiency. Pharmacotherapy. 2017. PMID: 28976587.; McNicholas BA, Pham MH, et al. Treatment of hyperkalemia with a low-dose insulin protocol is effective and results in reduced hypoglycemia. Kidney Int Rep. 2018. doi:10.1016/j.ekir.2017.10.009.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: ESRD with hyperkalemia for fistula declot

questions.stem: Same ESRD patient weighs 80 kg. Calcium gluconate 10% (100 mg/mL) is given for ECG changes. What volume provides 3 g?
questions.explanation: 3,000 mg ÷ 100 mg/mL = 30 mL. 3 mL is a decimal slip. 300 mL assumes 10 mg/mL. 10 mL gives 1 g.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: ESRD with hyperkalemia for fistula declot

questions.stem: Patient with BMI 55 is having sleeve gastrectomy. Match each drug to the weight scalar commonly used for dosing.
questions.explanation: Propofol induction is dosed to lean body weight because brain exposure follows lean tissue and cardiac output; succinylcholine to total weight because plasma cholinesterase and ECF rise with size; rocuronium to ideal weight because it stays mainly in lean tissue. Sugammadex is labeled for actual body weight. Body surface area isn't used for these drugs.

questions.stem: Same bariatric patient weighs 160 kg and is 170 cm tall. What is the BMI?
questions.explanation: BMI = kg ÷ m² = 160 ÷ 1.7² = 160 ÷ 2.89 ≈ 55. 94 divides by 1.7 instead of 1.7². 33 uses 220 lb. 64 uses 2.5 as the denominator.

questions.stem: 52-year-old man with BMI 37, neck 44 cm, hypertension, loud snoring, and daytime fatigue; no observed apneas. What is his STOP-BANG score?
questions.explanation: Snoring 1, Tired 1, Observed apneas 0, Pressure 1, BMI >35 1, Age >50 1, Neck >40 cm 1, Gender male 1 = 7. 6 misses one item. 8 counts observed apneas. 5 drops two items.

questions.stem: Same bariatric patient with STOP-BANG 7. Which postoperative analgesic plan BEST lowers respiratory risk?
options: Long-acting oral oxycodone started in PACU at low dose
Hydromorphone PCA with a basal infusion
questions.explanation: High OSA risk calls for opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with monitoring. Basal PCA infusions, long-acting opioids, and scheduled IM morphine all raise the risk of respiratory depression.

questions.stem: Patient receives monthly extended-release naltrexone for alcohol use disorder; last injection 2 weeks ago. She needs urgent ORIF of the wrist. Which analgesic plan is BEST?
options: Naloxone to displace naltrexone before opioids
Methadone loading to overcome the receptor blockade
questions.explanation: Naltrexone occupies mu receptors for weeks after injection, so usual opioid doses may fail; a block and nonopioid analgesics avoid the problem. If opioids are needed, very high doses with close monitoring are risky. Naloxone doesn't displace naltrexone usefully. Methadone faces the same blockade.

questions.stem: Same patient on naltrexone. Why is overcoming the blockade with large opioid doses dangerous?
options: Naltrexone converts opioids to neurotoxic metabolites
questions.explanation: As naltrexone wanes, the high opioid doses needed to break through can cause sudden, severe respiratory depression. The other mechanisms aren't real.

questions.stem: Patient takes prednisone 20 mg daily for lupus and is having a hemicolectomy. On induction BP drops to 72/38 and doesn't respond to phenylephrine. She skipped this morning's dose. Next drug?
questions.explanation: Refractory hypotension in a steroid-dependent patient suggests adrenal insufficiency; hydrocortisone restores vascular responsiveness. More phenylephrine doesn't treat the cause. Low-dose dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid effect. Oral fludrocortisone is slow.

questions.stem: 88-year-old, 50 kg, needs a fascia iliaca block with ropivacaine 0.2%. Using 3 mg/kg as the maximum, what is the largest volume?
questions.explanation: 3 × 50 = 150 mg. 0.2% = 2 mg/mL. 150 ÷ 2 = 75 mL; most blocks use far less. 7.5 mL is a decimal slip. 30 mL uses 0.5%. 150 mL gives milligrams as milliliters.

questions.stem: Same 88-year-old with dementia and a hip fracture. Which drugs raise postoperative delirium risk and are best avoided? (Select 4)
options: Ropivacaine for a fascia iliaca block
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines, anticholinergic antihistamines, scopolamine, and meperidine are on the Beers list for delirium risk. Acetaminophen and regional analgesia reduce opioid needs and may lower delirium.

questions.stem: Same 88-year-old. Sevoflurane MAC at age 40 is about 2.0% and falls about 6% per decade. What is her approximate MAC?
questions.explanation: 88 − 40 = 4.8 decades × 6% ≈ 29% lower: 2.0 × 0.71 ≈ 1.4%. 2.0% ignores age. 0.9% overestimates the decline. 1.8% uses a single decade.

questions.stem: Same 88-year-old in PACU after hip pinning: pain 7/10, mildly confused. Which analgesic approach is BEST?
options: Meperidine 50 mg IV for pain and shivering
Redose the block or give acetaminophen
questions.explanation: Regional analgesia and acetaminophen reduce opioid needs and delirium in older adults. Large morphine doses risk respiratory depression and delirium. Meperidine and diazepam raise delirium risk.

questions.stem: Patient with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) and CKD stage 4 needs urgent laparotomy. Which relaxant is BEST?
questions.explanation: Hofmann elimination is independent of liver and kidney function. Rocuronium depends on biliary clearance, and vecuronium and pancuronium depend on both organs.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Liver and kidney failure for urgent surgery

questions.stem: Same cirrhosis and CKD patient needs an opioid for maintenance. Which is BEST?
questions.explanation: Remifentanil's esterase clearance is unaffected by organ failure. Morphine and meperidine metabolites accumulate in kidney failure. High-dose hydromorphone risks H3G accumulation.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Liver and kidney failure for urgent surgery

questions.stem: Same patient needs sedation for EGD before surgery. Which benzodiazepine is BEST suited?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is cleared by tissue esterases to an inactive metabolite. Diazepam has an active long-acting metabolite. Midazolam's metabolite accumulates in kidney failure. Lorazepam infusions carry propylene glycol risk.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Liver and kidney failure for urgent surgery

questions.stem: Heart transplant recipient is having a hernia repair. Which response to hypovolemia should you anticipate?
options: Stable cardiac output despite moderate blood loss
A slow HR rise driven by circulating catecholamines
questions.explanation: The denervated heart can't mount a fast reflex HR response; it increases output first through preload (Frank-Starling) and later through circulating catecholamines. Vagal reflexes are absent.

questions.stem: Same heart transplant recipient. Which drugs act directly on the heart and keep their effect? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Direct agonists act on cardiac receptors regardless of innervation. Atropine and glycopyrrolate act through the vagus, which is cut. Ephedrine's indirect effect depends on nerve terminals, though its weaker direct component remains.

questions.stem: Patient takes echothiophate eye drops for glaucoma and needs RSI. Which relaxant is MOST affected?
questions.explanation: Echothiophate is an organophosphate that inhibits plasma cholinesterase for weeks, prolonging succinylcholine. The others aren't cleared by that enzyme.

questions.stem: Patient on apomorphine for Parkinson disease has PONV. Which antiemetic is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: 5-HT3 antagonists with apomorphine have caused profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. Dexamethasone and aprepitant are reasonable. Scopolamine raises delirium concerns but isn't contraindicated with apomorphine.

questions.stem: Patient takes aprepitant for chemotherapy-induced nausea and an oral contraceptive. Which counseling is MOST appropriate?
options: Use backup contraception for about a month
Increase the contraceptive dose for one week
questions.explanation: Aprepitant's enzyme effects lower contraceptive levels, and backup is advised during and for about 28 days after use. Dose increases aren't recommended. Stopping isn't needed for surgery.

questions.stem: Patient takes ezetimibe and atorvastatin. What is the perioperative plan?
options: Stop the statin and continue ezetimibe
Hold both and restart at 1 month to limit myopathy
Continue the statin; ezetimibe is optional
questions.explanation: Continuing statins lowers perioperative cardiovascular risk and stopping can cause rebound. Ezetimibe has no specific perioperative risk. Long holds lose the benefit.

questions.stem: Patient takes niacin and reports flushing. Which perioperative drug reduces niacin flushing?
questions.explanation: Niacin flushing is prostaglandin-mediated, so a dose of aspirin about 30 min beforehand blunts it. Ondansetron, famotidine, and metoclopramide act on serotonin, histamine H2, and dopamine pathways, none of which drive niacin flushing.

questions.stem: Patient on fenofibrate and simvastatin has diffuse muscle pain and dark urine before elective surgery. What is the BEST step?
options: Proceed; myalgias are common with statins
Check CK and creatinine; consider delay
Proceed with succinylcholine RSI and check CK afterward
questions.explanation: Fibrate plus statin raises rhabdomyolysis risk, and myalgias with dark urine warrant CK, creatinine, and potassium checks before elective surgery. Succinylcholine could cause hyperkalemia if rhabdomyolysis is present. Dantrolene isn't indicated.

questions.stem: 68-year-old in PACU after hip surgery got hydromorphone 2 mg and midazolam 2 mg; rocuronium was reversed. RR 6, pinpoint pupils, TOF ratio 0.95. Which finding points AWAY from residual block?
questions.explanation: A TOF ratio above 0.9 indicates adequate neuromuscular recovery. Miosis and slow breathing point to opioid effect. The midazolam dose suggests a sedative contribution, not neuromuscular weakness.

questions.stem: Same 68-year-old after naloxone 120 mcg total: RR 14 now, but she is still hard to rouse with SpO2 92%. She also got midazolam 2 mg. Which drug is MOST reasonable?
questions.explanation: Persistent sedation after opioid reversal in a patient who received a benzodiazepine suggests a residual benzodiazepine effect; small flumazenil doses can help if she isn't benzodiazepine-dependent. More naloxone risks pain and a surge. Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity. Doxapram isn't first-line.

questions.stem: Same patient: 45 min later RR falls to 7 again. She needed 0.12 mg naloxone total to respond. Using two-thirds of the effective dose per hour, what infusion rate is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds × 0.12 = 0.08 mg/hr. 0.12 gives the full dose hourly. 0.8 is a decimal slip. 0.04 uses one-third.

questions.stem: 25-year-old thrashes and pulls at lines on emergence after nasal surgery. SpO2 94%. What is the FIRST step?
options: Exclude hypoxemia, pain, and a full bladder
Physical restraints for safety while preparing a sedative
questions.explanation: Agitation can be the first sign of hypoxemia, hypercarbia, pain, or bladder distension, which drugs can mask. Treat causes first; sedation comes after. Restraints alone don't address cause and can harm.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Emergence delirium in a young adult

questions.stem: Same 25-year-old: treatable causes are excluded and agitation persists. Which drug is BEST?
options: Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV, then reassess in 5 min
questions.explanation: Dex calms without much respiratory depression; give it slowly and watch for bradycardia and hypotension. Midazolam can worsen disorientation. Physostigmine is for anticholinergic toxicity. Ketamine can cause emergence reactions.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Emergence delirium in a young adult

questions.stem: PACU patient with BP 182/98 and HR 104 after open abdominal surgery. Which causes should be checked before giving an antihypertensive? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Pain, urinary retention, hypoxemia, hypercarbia, and missed home medications (especially clonidine or beta blockers) commonly raise BP after surgery. Hypothermia causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.

questions.stem: After spinal anesthesia for TURP, a 75-year-old shivers vigorously; core temp is 35.4 °C. What is the BEST plan?
options: Ondansetron 4 mg IV and observation without warming
questions.explanation: Shivering after spinal is driven by heat redistribution and real hypothermia, so warming treats the cause and small meperidine doses (12.5–25 mg) control symptoms. 50 mg is excessive for an older adult. Dantrolene isn't used. Ondansetron alone has limited effect.

questions.stem: After interscalene block for shoulder surgery, a patient with COPD reports dyspnea; SpO2 89% on 2 L. Breath sounds are reduced at the right base. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Interscalene blocks nearly always affect the phrenic nerve, causing hemidiaphragm paresis that patients with poor reserve tolerate badly. Pneumothorax is rare with ultrasound. LAST causes CNS symptoms first. High spinal causes widespread block.

questions.stem: Same patient with COPD needs shoulder analgesia. Which block choice reduces phrenic involvement?
options: Supraclavicular block with 40 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%
questions.explanation: Superior trunk and suprascapular approaches spare the phrenic nerve more often than interscalene. Higher volumes increase phrenic spread. A deep cervical plexus block often blocks the phrenic nerve.

questions.stem: During an interscalene block with 20 mL ropivacaine 0.5%, the patient suddenly loses consciousness and becomes apneic; BP 70/40. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Injection near the cervical neuraxis can spread intrathecally, causing total spinal with apnea and hypotension. Phrenic block causes dyspnea, not unconsciousness. Vasovagal reactions don't cause apnea. Horner syndrome is a benign sign of stellate spread.

questions.stem: A TAP block with liposomal bupivacaine is planned after 20 mL of 0.5% plain bupivacaine was infiltrated. What dosing principle applies?
options: They can be given together without dose limits of any kind
Allowed if plain dose is under half the liposomal dose
questions.explanation: Labeling allows plain bupivacaine with liposomal bupivacaine when the plain dose doesn't exceed 50% of the liposomal dose, and they can be given together. Other local anesthetics need a 20-min gap. Plain bupivacaine doesn't block release.

questions.stem: Outpatient needs a spinal for knee arthroscopy and wants to go home within a few hours. Which choice offers a short duration with low TNS risk?
questions.explanation: Mepivacaine provides an intermediate-duration spinal with lower TNS risk than lidocaine. Hyperbaric 5% lidocaine has the highest TNS association. Bupivacaine 15 mg and tetracaine with epinephrine last too long.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Mepivacaine spinal for ambulatory knee arthroscopy

questions.stem: Same outpatient: why is mepivacaine avoided for obstetric epidurals?
options: It is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase
questions.explanation: Neonates metabolize mepivacaine poorly, so its half-life is prolonged and accumulation occurs. It doesn't stimulate the uterus. It is an amide, and it does cross the placenta.

sourceMeta.caseTitle: Mepivacaine spinal for ambulatory knee arthroscopy

questions.stem: Patient on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, last dose 48 hr ago, CrCl 30, scheduled for spinal anesthesia. What is the BEST plan?
options: Check INR and proceed if under 1.5 with a smaller needle
questions.explanation: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily is a high (therapeutic) dose, and ASRA guidance holds it about 72 hr before neuraxial block; renal impairment argues for caution or a drug-specific level. The 2025 fifth edition allows a shorter 36-hr hold for low-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily), which doesn't apply here. INR doesn't reflect apixaban effect, and reversal for an elective spinal isn't appropriate.
questions.citation: Kopp SL, Vandermeulen E, McBane RD, Perlas A, Leffert L, Horlocker T. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine evidence-based guidelines (fifth edition). Reg Anesth Pain Med. Published online October 16, 2025. doi:10.1136/rapm-2024-105766.; Horlocker TT, Vandermeulen E, Kopp SL, et al. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy: ASRA evidence-based guidelines (fourth edition). Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2018;43(3):263-309.

questions.stem: Patient on prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily took the last dose 14 hr ago. Can an epidural be placed?
options: No; wait 24 hr for any LMWH
Yes, but use a 25-gauge needle to limit trauma
questions.explanation: ASRA guidance requires at least 12 hr after a prophylactic LMWH dose and 24 hr after a therapeutic dose. Anti-Xa levels aren't routinely required for prophylactic dosing. Needle gauge doesn't change the timing guidance.
questions.citation: Horlocker TT, Vandermeulen E, Kopp SL, et al. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy: ASRA evidence-based guidelines (fourth edition). Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2018;43(3):263-309.; Kopp SL, Vandermeulen E, McBane RD, Perlas A, Leffert L, Horlocker T. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine evidence-based guidelines (fifth edition). Reg Anesth Pain Med. Published online October 16, 2025. doi:10.1136/rapm-2024-105766.

questions.stem: Match each drug to the usual interval before restarting it after epidural catheter removal.
questions.explanation: ASRA guidance: prophylactic LMWH no sooner than 4 hr after catheter removal; IV heparin 1 hr after removal; low-dose DOACs such as apixaban 2.5 mg 6 hr after removal (the 2025 fifth edition extends this to 24 hr for high, therapeutic doses); clopidogrel immediately if no loading dose, or 6 hr after removal if a load is given. 48 hr isn't a standard restart interval for these.
questions.citation: Kopp SL, Vandermeulen E, McBane RD, Perlas A, Leffert L, Horlocker T.
